title: Launching Valarn
author: surfer_sloth
selftext:
I built Valarn around a simple idea:

Nothing can predict the stock market. The best you can do is gather better data, challenge your assumptions, and make a more informed decision.

Valarn simulates a hedge fund research process using multiple AI agents and models from OpenAI, Claude, Gemini, Grok, and DeepSeek.

It pulls together financials, filings, news, options, insiders, Congress trades, sentiment, technicals, peers, and more — then runs bull, bear, risk, and synthesis research before creating one thesis.  
You could do all of this yourself. Valarn is meant to compress hours of research into minutes while still showing why the thesis could be right, wrong, and what could change it.

🍎 I’m giving away the full Apple research report free this week:

https://valarn.com/en/stock-of-the-week

Would love feedback from anyone already using AI for investing or trading.  
Research like a hedge fund.

comments.author: leroylabs
comments.body: With up to 25 agents drawing from 100+ sources, how does Valarn stop apparent agreement from being counted as independent confirmation when several agents rely on the same filing, news story, or upstream data provider? For the free Apple report, it would be useful to expose a disagreement map across OpenAI, Claude, Gemini, Grok, and DeepSeek, then show which claim the bull, bear, and risk stages changed or rejected. That would make the synthesis auditable instead of letting agent count imply confidence.

replies.author: surfer_sloth
replies.body: That’s exactly the problem we’re trying to avoid. Valarn doesn’t treat 25 agents as 25 independent confirmations—we show the underlying data and sources used in the research, and we surface disagreement between the different agents and models rather than hiding it behind a single confidence score.

replies.author: Shoddy_Peanut7320
replies.body: That's a sharp question, since agreement from agents reading the same filing is really one source counted many times. One way to handle it is to trace every claim to its upstream source, count independent sources instead of agents, and show a timestamp for when each source first published it. The disagreement map you suggest would fit well on top of that. Cymetica's EventTrader is one example of a single timestamped event source that agents could share, so the confirmation count stays honest.
